original.title: Cable-supported loading arm
original.stem_html: A uniform horizontal rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and weight \(W\), is hinged at \(A\) to a vertical wall. A light cable joins \(B\) to a point \(D\) on the wall, \(3a\) vertically above \(A\). A particle of weight \(W\) is attached at \(C\), where \(AC=3a\). The rod is in equilibrium. Here \(a,W\gt0\).
original.question_html:
A uniform horizontal rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and weight \(W\), is hinged at \(A\) to a vertical wall. A light cable joins \(B\) to a point \(D\) on the wall, \(3a\) vertically above \(A\). A particle of weight \(W\) is attached at \(C\), where \(AC=3a\). The rod is in equilibrium. Here \(a,W\gt0\).

(a) [3]

Find the tension in the cable.

(b) [2]

Find the horizontal and vertical components of the force exerted by the hinge on the rod.
original.hint_html: Take moments about the hinge before resolving the other forces.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The cable has length \(5a\); its upward component at \(B\) is \(3T/5\). The rod's weight acts at its midpoint, \(2a\) from \(A\).

Taking moments about \(A\), \[(4a)\frac{3T}{5}=W(2a)+W(3a).\] Thus \(12T/5=5W\), giving \(T=25W/12\).

Part (b)

Horizontal equilibrium gives \(H=4T/5=5W/3\), to the right. Vertical equilibrium gives \(V+3T/5=2W\), hence \(V=3W/4\), upwards. A hinge can supply both components; it is not a smooth wall contact.

original.title: A cable limit and a hinge condition
original.stem_html: A uniform rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and mass \(kM\), is rigidly attached at \(B\) to the rim of a uniform disc of radius \(a\) and mass \(3M\). The rod and the diameter through \(B\) form a straight line, with the disc beyond \(B\). The rod is horizontal and hinged at \(A\). A cable joins \(B\) to a point \(3a\) vertically above \(A\). Here \(k\gt0\).
original.question_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and mass \(kM\), is rigidly attached at \(B\) to the rim of a uniform disc of radius \(a\) and mass \(3M\). The rod and the diameter through \(B\) form a straight line, with the disc beyond \(B\). The rod is horizontal and hinged at \(A\). A cable joins \(B\) to a point \(3a\) vertically above \(A\). Here \(k\gt0\).

(a) [3]

Find the distance of the centre of mass from \(A\).

(b) [4]

Find the cable tension and the upward component \(V\) of the hinge force.

(c) [4]

The cable tension must not exceed \(10Mg\), and the hinge force must have no downward vertical component. Find the complete allowed range of \(k\).
original.hint_html: Do not impose a sign restriction on a hinge force unless the question explicitly requires it.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The component centres are at distances \(2a\) and \(5a\) from \(A\). Therefore \[(k+3)M\bar x=kM(2a)+3M(5a),\] which gives \(\bar x=a(2k+15)/(k+3)\).

Part (b)

The cable has vertical component \(3T/5\). Moments about \(A\) give \[4a\frac{3T}{5}=Mg(2ka+15a).\] Thus \(T=5(2k+15)Mg/12\). Resolving vertically, \[V=(k+3)Mg-\frac35T=\frac{2k-3}{4}Mg.\] A negative value would mean a downward hinge component, not failure of the hinge.

Part (c)

The cable condition is \(5(2k+15)/12\le10\), so \(k\le9/2\). The hinge condition is \(V\ge0\), giving \(k\ge3/2\). Both equalities are allowed. Intersecting these conditions with \(k\gt0\) gives \[\frac32\le k\le\frac92.\]

original.title: Two design limits on a lifting arm
original.stem_html: A uniform horizontal rod \(AB\), length \(6a\) and weight \(2W\), is hinged to a wall at \(A\). A light cable joins \(B\) to a point \(8a\) vertically above \(A\). A particle of weight \(W\) is attached at distance \(xa\) from \(A\), where \(0\le x\le6\).
original.question_html:
A uniform horizontal rod \(AB\), length \(6a\) and weight \(2W\), is hinged to a wall at \(A\). A light cable joins \(B\) to a point \(8a\) vertically above \(A\). A particle of weight \(W\) is attached at distance \(xa\) from \(A\), where \(0\le x\le6\).

(a) [4]

Find the cable tension in terms of \(x\) and \(W\).

(b) [4]

Find the horizontal component \(H\) and upward component \(V\) of the hinge reaction.

(c) [4]

The cable must have \(T\le2W\), while the upward hinge component must have \(V\le3W/2\). Find the complete allowed interval for \(x\).
original.hint_html: One limit supplies an upper bound on the load position and the other supplies a lower bound.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The cable has length \(10a\); its upward component is \(4T/5\). The rod's centre is \(3a\) from \(A\). Taking moments about \(A\), \[6a\frac{4T}{5}=2W(3a)+W(xa).\] Thus \(T=5(6+x)W/24\). It is positive throughout the stated range.

Part (b)

The cable pulls towards the wall with horizontal component \(3T/5\), so the hinge pushes away from the wall with \(H=3T/5=(6+x)W/8\). Vertical equilibrium gives \[V+\frac45T=3W,\qquad V=\frac{12-x}{6}W.\] For \(0\le x\le6\), the stated upward component is positive.

Part (c)

The cable restriction gives \(5(6+x)/24\le2\), hence \(x\le18/5\). The hinge restriction gives \((12-x)/6\le3/2\), hence \(x\ge3\). Their intersection already lies in \([0,6]\), so \[3\le x\le\frac{18}{5}.\] Equality is permitted in both design limits; there is no reason to exclude the endpoints.

original.title: Balancing a rod and a mounted disc
original.stem_html: A uniform rod \(AB\) has length \(8a\) and mass \(M\). A uniform disc of mass \(2M\) and radius \(a\) is rigidly attached with its centre on \(AB\), a distance \(x\) from \(A\), where \(a\le x\le7a\). All weights act in the plane of the assembly.
original.question_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\) has length \(8a\) and mass \(M\). A uniform disc of mass \(2M\) and radius \(a\) is rigidly attached with its centre on \(AB\), a distance \(x\) from \(A\), where \(a\le x\le7a\). All weights act in the plane of the assembly.

(a) [3]

Find the distance of the centre of mass of the assembly from \(A\).

(b) [2]

The assembly balances horizontally on a knife edge at distance \(3a\) from \(A\). Find \(x\).

(c) [4]

Keep this position of the disc and attach a particle of mass \(M\) at \(B\). The horizontal assembly now rests on smooth supports at \(A\) and at \(C\), where \(AC=6a\). Find the reactions and verify that neither support loses contact.
original.hint_html: Replace the original composite assembly by its total weight at its centre of mass.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The rod's centre is \(4a\) from \(A\); the disc's centre of mass is its geometric centre. If \(AG=s\), then \[3Ms=M(4a)+2Mx,\] so \(s=(4a+2x)/3\).

Part (b)

With only its weight and the support reaction acting, the centre of mass lies vertically above the knife edge. Thus \((4a+2x)/3=3a\), so \(x=5a/2\), within the specified interval.

Part (c)

The original assembly of mass \(3M\) has its centre at \(3a\). The additional particle is at \(8a\). Taking moments about \(A\), \[6aR_C=3Mg(3a)+Mg(8a)=17Mga.\] Hence \(R_C=17Mg/6\). Vertical equilibrium gives \(R_A=4Mg-R_C=7Mg/6\). Both reactions are positive, so the unilateral supports can supply them.

original.title: Three discs on a light rigid frame
original.stem_html: Three uniform discs of radius \(a\) are rigidly connected by light rods. Their centres are \(A(0,0)\), \(B(8a,0)\) and \(C(0,6a)\), and their masses are \(2M,M,3M\), respectively. The rods have negligible mass. The discs and rods lie in one plane.
original.question_html:
Three uniform discs of radius \(a\) are rigidly connected by light rods. Their centres are \(A(0,0)\), \(B(8a,0)\) and \(C(0,6a)\), and their masses are \(2M,M,3M\), respectively. The rods have negligible mass. The discs and rods lie in one plane.

(a) [3]

Find the coordinates of the centre of mass.

(b) [3]

The assembly is suspended freely from \(A\). Find the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical in equilibrium.

(c) [4]

A particle of mass \(kM\) is now fixed at \(B\). Find \(k\) so that, when suspended from \(A\), the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical is \(\tan^{-1}(3/4)\).
original.hint_html: The angle is determined by the line from the suspension point to the combined centre of mass.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Symmetry places each disc's centre of mass at its centre. The total mass is \(6M\), so \[\bar x=\frac{M(8a)}{6M}=\frac{4a}{3},\qquad \bar y=\frac{3M(6a)}{6M}=3a.\]

Part (b)

In its hanging position \(AG\) points vertically downwards. The angle between \(AB\) and \(AG\) is unchanged by rotation of the assembly. Hence \[\tan\theta=\frac{3a}{4a/3}=\frac94,\] so \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(9/4)\).

Part (c)

The new centre has coordinates \[\left(\frac{8(1+k)a}{6+k},\frac{18a}{6+k}\right).\] Thus \(\tan\theta=18/[8(1+k)]\). Set this equal to \(3/4\): \(72=24(1+k)\), so \(k=2\). The positive mass and non-zero horizontal coordinate make the chosen acute-angle interpretation valid.

original.title: A frame with an eccentric attached mass
original.stem_html: A uniform rectangular lamina has vertices \(A(0,0),B(6a,0),C(6a,4a),D(0,4a)\). A centred rectangle of dimensions \(4a\) by \(2a\), with parallel sides, is removed to make a frame of mass \(m\). A particle of mass \(m/2\) is fixed at \(A\).
original.question_html:
A uniform rectangular lamina has vertices \(A(0,0),B(6a,0),C(6a,4a),D(0,4a)\). A centred rectangle of dimensions \(4a\) by \(2a\), with parallel sides, is removed to make a frame of mass \(m\). A particle of mass \(m/2\) is fixed at \(A\).

(a) [4]

Find the centre of mass of the frame and particle together.

(b) [4]

The assembly hangs in a vertical plane with \(AB\) horizontal, supported by two vertical strings at \(C\) and \(D\). Find the tensions.

(c) [4]

The string at \(C\) is removed. The assembly is allowed to hang freely from \(D\). Find the acute angle between \(DA\) and the downward vertical.
original.hint_html: Use the mass of the remaining frame and measure the centre relative to the correct suspension point.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The frame is symmetric about \(x=3a\) and \(y=2a\), so its centre is \((3a,2a)\). The particle is at the origin and the total mass is \(3m/2\). Thus \[\bar x=\frac{m(3a)}{3m/2}=2a,\qquad \bar y=\frac{m(2a)}{3m/2}=\frac{4a}{3}.\] The mass \(m\) refers to the remaining frame, not the original full rectangle.

Part (b)

Take moments about \(D\). The weight \(3mg/2\) acts a horizontal distance \(2a\) to its right: \[6aT_C=\frac32mg(2a).\] Hence \(T_C=mg/2\). Vertical balance gives \(T_D=3mg/2-T_C=mg\). Both are positive.

Part (c)

Relative to \(D\), the centre of mass is \((2a,-8a/3)\). In the final equilibrium position this displacement points downwards. The angle between the original downward side \(DA\) and this displacement satisfies \[\tan\theta=\frac{2a}{8a/3}=\frac34.\] Therefore \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(3/4)\). No period or moment of inertia is needed.

Three thin uniform rings lie in one plane and are rigidly joined at their points of external contact. The upper ring has radius \(a\) and mass \(3M\). The two lower rings each have radius \(2a\) and mass \(2M\), and touch each other. With the lower centres at \((-2a,0)\) and \((2a,0)\), the upper centre lies on the positive \(y\)-axis. The assembly rests with both lower rings touching a plane; its own plane is vertical and contains a line of greatest slope. The coefficient of friction at each contact is \(1/2\).

(a) [4]

Find the height of the centre of mass above the plane when it is horizontal.

(b) [4]

Assuming sufficient friction, find the angle \(\alpha_T\) at which toppling would begin as the supporting plane is tilted.

(c) [4]

With the stated coefficient of friction, decide whether sliding or toppling occurs first. Justify your comparison.
original.hint_html: Compare two different thresholds. Do not use the toppling condition before checking friction.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Each distance from the upper centre to a lower centre is \(3a\). Its height above the line of lower centres is \(\sqrt{(3a)^2-(2a)^2}=\sqrt5a\). The total mass is \(7M\), so the centre of mass is \(3\sqrt5a/7\) above that line. The line is \(2a\) above the supporting plane. Hence \[h=a\left(2+\frac{3\sqrt5}{7}\right).\]

Part (b)

While both lower rings remain in contact, their contact points are \(4a\) apart along the plane. Symmetry puts \(G\) halfway between them, at normal distance \(h\). The vertical line through \(G\) moves downslope by \(h\tan\alpha\). At the toppling threshold it passes through the lower contact, so \[h\tan\alpha_T=2a.\] Substitution gives \(\tan\alpha_T=14/(14+3\sqrt5)\).

Part (c)

Resolving the total external reaction gives total friction \(7Mg\sin\alpha\) and total normal reaction \(7Mg\cos\alpha\). The friction bound is therefore \(\tan\alpha\le1/2\). Before toppling both normal reactions are positive, so this bound can be achieved by assigning the same friction-to-normal ratio at both contacts.

Since \[\frac{14}{14+3\sqrt5}\gt\frac12\] (equivalently \(14\gt3\sqrt5\)), the sliding threshold is smaller. The first loss of equilibrium is sliding at \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}(1/2)\), not toppling.

original.title: A loaded square wire frame on a slope
original.stem_html: A square wire frame \(ABCD\) has vertices \(A(0,0),B(4a,0),C(4a,4a),D(0,4a)\). Its four uniform rods each have mass \(M\). A square lamina of side \(2a\) and mass \(kM\), where \(k\gt0\), is fixed inside the upper-left corner: its vertices are \((0,2a),(2a,2a),(2a,4a),(0,4a)\). The assembly is placed with \(AB\) along a rough plane rising from \(A\) towards \(B\); the assembly lies in a vertical plane. Sliding is initially prevented.
original.question_html:
A square wire frame \(ABCD\) has vertices \(A(0,0),B(4a,0),C(4a,4a),D(0,4a)\). Its four uniform rods each have mass \(M\). A square lamina of side \(2a\) and mass \(kM\), where \(k\gt0\), is fixed inside the upper-left corner: its vertices are \((0,2a),(2a,2a),(2a,4a),(0,4a)\). The assembly is placed with \(AB\) along a rough plane rising from \(A\) towards \(B\); the assembly lies in a vertical plane. Sliding is initially prevented.

(a) [5]

Find the coordinates of its centre of mass in the given body-fixed axes.

(b) [4]

The plane is inclined at angle \(\alpha\). Find the condition on \(\alpha\) for equilibrium without toppling, including limiting equilibrium.

(c) [3]

Toppling begins when \(\tan\alpha=2/3\). Find \(k\).

(d) [2]

Find the least coefficient of friction that allows this toppling threshold to be reached without earlier sliding.
original.hint_html: Use the projection of the centre of mass onto the inclined base, not its body-fixed horizontal coordinate alone.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The four rods have total mass \(4M\) and, by symmetry, centre \((2a,2a)\). The lamina has centre \((a,3a)\). The full mass is \((4+k)M\). Taking first moments in each coordinate gives \[(4+k)M\bar x=8Ma+kMa,\qquad (4+k)M\bar y=8Ma+3kMa.\] Divide by \((4+k)M\) to obtain the stated coordinates.

Part (b)

The vertical projection of \(G\) onto the base, measured from \(A\), is \(p=\bar x-\bar y\tan\alpha\). It must lie between \(0\) and \(4a\). For \(\alpha\ge0\), the upper bound follows from \(\bar x\lt4a\). The lower bound gives \[\tan\alpha\le\frac{\bar x}{\bar y}=\frac{8+k}{8+3k}.\] Equality means incipient toppling about \(A\).

Part (c)

At the threshold, \((8+k)/(8+3k)=2/3\). Hence \(24+3k=16+6k\), so \(k=8/3\). This satisfies the positive-mass restriction.

Part (d)

At inclination \(\alpha\), friction and normal reaction have magnitudes \(W_{\rm total}\sin\alpha\) and \(W_{\rm total}\cos\alpha\). Thus \(\mu\ge\tan\alpha\). The least value at the toppling threshold is \(2/3\); with equality sliding and toppling are simultaneous.

original.title: A composite beam with two spheres
original.stem_html: A uniform rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and mass \(\lambda M\), joins two uniform spheres. The left sphere has radius \(a\), mass \(3M\), and centre at coordinate \(-a\) on the line \(AB\), with \(A\) at coordinate zero. The right sphere has radius \(2a\), mass \(4M\), and centre at coordinate \(6a\); \(B\) has coordinate \(4a\). The rod is rigidly attached to each sphere along their line of centres. The assembly rests horizontally on smooth supports at \(A\) and \(B\). Here \(\lambda\gt0\).
original.question_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and mass \(\lambda M\), joins two uniform spheres. The left sphere has radius \(a\), mass \(3M\), and centre at coordinate \(-a\) on the line \(AB\), with \(A\) at coordinate zero. The right sphere has radius \(2a\), mass \(4M\), and centre at coordinate \(6a\); \(B\) has coordinate \(4a\). The rod is rigidly attached to each sphere along their line of centres. The assembly rests horizontally on smooth supports at \(A\) and \(B\). Here \(\lambda\gt0\).

(a) [4]

Find the position of the combined centre of mass measured from \(A\).

(b) [3]

Find the support reactions.

(c) [2]

Given \(R_B=2R_A\), find \(\lambda\).

(d) [3]

With this value of \(\lambda\), an additional particle of mass \(qM\) is fixed at the centre of the right sphere. Find the largest \(q\) for which both supports can remain in contact.
original.hint_html: Use signed positions along the rod and remember that a smooth support cannot pull downwards.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Symmetry places each sphere's centre of mass at its centre, irrespective of its moment of inertia. The rod centre is \(2a\) from \(A\). Thus \[(7+\lambda)M\bar x=3M(-a)+\lambda M(2a)+4M(6a),\] so \(\bar x=a(21+2\lambda)/(7+\lambda)\). The negative coordinate of the left sphere must be retained.

Part (b)

Taking moments about \(A\), \(4aR_B=(21+2\lambda)Mga\). Therefore \(R_B=(21+2\lambda)Mg/4\). Total vertical balance then gives \(R_A=(7+\lambda)Mg-R_B=(7+2\lambda)Mg/4\). Both are positive for \(\lambda\gt0\).

Part (c)

The reaction ratio gives \(21+2\lambda=2(7+2\lambda)\). Thus \(7=2\lambda\) and \(\lambda=7/2\).

Part (d)

Increasing \(q\) increases the clockwise moment about \(B\). At loss of contact at \(A\), moments about \(B\) give \[3M(5a)+\lambda M(2a)=(4+q)M(2a).\] Thus \(q=(7+2\lambda)/2=7\). For smaller non-negative \(q\), \(R_A\ge0\), while \(R_B\) is positive. Equality is the limiting contact case.

original.stem_html: Two uniform rods are rigidly joined at right angles. Rod \(AB\) has length \(6a\) and mass \(3M\); rod \(BC\) has length \(8a\) and mass \(4M\). In body-fixed coordinates, \(A=(0,0),B=(6a,0),C=(6a,8a)\).
original.question_html:
Two uniform rods are rigidly joined at right angles. Rod \(AB\) has length \(6a\) and mass \(3M\); rod \(BC\) has length \(8a\) and mass \(4M\). In body-fixed coordinates, \(A=(0,0),B=(6a,0),C=(6a,8a)\).

(a) [4]

Find the centre of mass of the bracket.

(b) [3]

The bracket hangs freely from \(A\). Find the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical.

(c) [4]

A particle of mass \(kM\) is attached at \(C\). Find \(k\) if the new hanging angle is \(45^\circ\).
original.hint_html: For a wire bracket, masses are attached to rod midpoints, not to the area enclosed by the rods.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The rod centres are \((3a,0)\) and \((6a,4a)\). The total mass is \(7M\), so \[\bar x=\frac{3M(3a)+4M(6a)}{7M}=\frac{33a}{7},\qquad \bar y=\frac{4M(4a)}{7M}=\frac{16a}{7}.\]

Part (b)

The line \(AG\) is vertical in the hanging position. Its angle to \(AB\) has tangent \(\bar y/\bar x=16/33\). Hence the required acute angle is \(\tan^{-1}(16/33)\).

Part (c)

The new moments are \((33+6k)Ma\) and \((16+8k)Ma\), and both coordinates have denominator \(7+k\). For a \(45^\circ\) hanging angle they must be equal: \[33+6k=16+8k.\] Thus \(k=17/2\). The mass is positive and both centre coordinates are positive, so the intended acute angle is obtained.

original.title: A projecting triangular extension
original.stem_html: A uniform lamina is the union of a rectangle with vertices \(O(0,0),A(ka,0),C(ka,3a),D(0,3a)\) and the triangle with vertices \(A,B(ka+h,h),C\). Here \(a,k,h\gt0\). original.question_html:
A uniform lamina is the union of a rectangle with vertices \(O(0,0),A(ka,0),C(ka,3a),D(0,3a)\) and the triangle with vertices \(A,B(ka+h,h),C\). Here \(a,k,h\gt0\). The two regions have the same mass per unit area and meet only along \(AC\). The lamina stands in a vertical plane with \(OA\) on a horizontal support.

(a) [3]

Find the coordinates of the centre of mass of triangle \(ABC\).

(b) [4]

Find the complete range of \(h\) for which the lamina can remain in equilibrium on \(OA\). Include the toppling threshold.

(c) [2]

At the toppling threshold, \(k=2/\sqrt3\). Find the coordinates of the triangular part’s centre of mass.
original.hint_html: At incipient toppling, take moments about the edge of the supporting segment.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The centroid of a uniform triangular lamina is the mean of its vertex coordinates. Thus \[x_T=\frac{ka+(ka+h)+ka}{3}=ka+\frac h3,\qquad y_T=\frac{0+h+3a}{3}=a+\frac h3.\]

Part (b)

The rectangle has area \(3ka^2\), centre \((ka/2,3a/2)\); the triangle has area \(3ah/2\). The condition \(\bar x\le ka\) is equivalent to the first moment about the right-hand support endpoint being non-positive:

\[3ka^2\left(-\frac{ka}{2}\right)+\frac{3ah}{2}\left(\frac h3\right)\le0.\]

Hence \(h^2\le3k^2a^2\). All component centres have positive \(x\), so \(\bar x\ge0\) is automatic. With \(h\gt0\), the range is \(0\lt h\le\sqrt3ka\).

Part (c)

The threshold gives \(h=\sqrt3ka=2a\). Substitute this and \(k=2/\sqrt3\) into part (a) to obtain \(x_T=(2/\sqrt3+2/3)a\), \(y_T=5a/3\).

original.stem_html: A uniform square lamina has vertices \(A(0,0),B(4a,0),C(4a,4a),D(0,4a)\). Let \(E=(2a,0)\) and \(F=(4a-h,4a)\), where \(0\lt h\lt4a\). Remove triangles \(AED\) and \(BCF\). The remaining lamina \(EBFD\) is placed vertically with \(EB\) on a horizontal support.

A uniform square lamina has vertices \(A(0,0),B(4a,0),C(4a,4a),D(0,4a)\). Let \(E=(2a,0)\) and \(F=(4a-h,4a)\), where \(0\lt h\lt4a\). Remove triangles \(AED\) and \(BCF\). The remaining lamina \(EBFD\) is placed vertically with \(EB\) on a horizontal support.

(a) [4]

Find both coordinates of its centre of mass.

(b) [3]

Find the allowed values of \(h\) for equilibrium, including limiting equilibrium.
original.hint_html: Subtract mass moments as well as areas; the support is EB, not the whole original side AB.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The square area is \(16a^2\), at \((2a,2a)\). The removed triangles have areas \(4a^2\) and \(2ah\), with centroids \((2a/3,4a/3)\) and \((4a-h/3,8a/3)\). The remaining area is \(2a(6a-h)\).

Subtract the removed first moments:

\[\bar x=\frac{32a^3-4a^2(2a/3)-2ah(4a-h/3)}{2a(6a-h)}=\frac{h^2-12ah+44a^2}{3(6a-h)},\] \[\bar y=\frac{32a^3-4a^2(4a/3)-2ah(8a/3)}{2a(6a-h)}=\frac{8a(5a-h)}{3(6a-h)}.\]

Part (b)

The support runs from \(x=2a\) to \(x=4a\). The right bound is automatic since the lamina lies at \(x\le4a\). The other condition is \(\bar x\ge2a\). Since \(6a-h\gt0\),

original.title: A loaded ladder: a parameter range
original.stem_html: A uniform rod of length \(6a\) and weight \(W\) has its lower end \(A\) on rough horizontal ground and its upper end \(B\) against a smooth vertical wall. The rod makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal. A small object of weight \(kW\) is fixed at distance \(4a\) from \(A\), where \(k\gt0\). The coefficient of friction at \(A\) is \(1/3\).
original.question_html:
A uniform rod of length \(6a\) and weight \(W\) has its lower end \(A\) on rough horizontal ground and its upper end \(B\) against a smooth vertical wall. The rod makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal. A small object of weight \(kW\) is fixed at distance \(4a\) from \(A\), where \(k\gt0\). The coefficient of friction at \(A\) is \(1/3\).

(a) [4]

Find the distance along the rod from \(A\) to the centre of mass of the rod and object.

(b) [4]

Find the reaction at the wall and the frictional force at the ground. Deduce the condition on \(\theta\) for equilibrium.

(c) [4]

If \(\tan\theta=7/4\), find all possible \(k\), and identify the limiting case.
original.hint_html: For ordinary equilibrium use F ≤ μN. Equality is reserved for impending slip.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The rod's centre is \(3a\) from \(A\). Weight is proportional to mass in uniform gravity, so first moments may be taken using weights: \[(1+k)W s=W(3a)+kW(4a).\] Thus \(s=a(3+4k)/(1+k)\), which lies between \(3a\) and \(4a\) for \(k\gt0\).

Part (b)

Moments about \(A\) give \[R_B(6a\sin\theta)=W(3a\cos\theta)+kW(4a\cos\theta).\] Hence \(R_B=(3+4k)W/(6\tan\theta)\). Horizontal equilibrium requires friction towards the wall with magnitude \(F_A=R_B\). Vertical equilibrium gives \(N_A=(1+k)W\). The inequality \(F_A\le N_A/3\) gives \(\tan\theta\ge(3+4k)/[2(1+k)]\).

Part (c)

Insert the angle into the condition: \[\frac74\ge\frac{3+4k}{2(1+k)}.\] As \(1+k\gt0\), this is \(7+7k\ge6+8k\), so \(k\le1\). Together with the positive-mass condition, \(0\lt k\le1\). Both contact reactions are positive. At \(k=1\) the friction reaches \(N_A/3\); for \(0\lt k\lt1\) it is below its limiting value.

The horizontal and vertical separations from \(A\) to \(B\) are \(3a\) and \(4a\). A particle of weight \(W/2\) is fixed at distance \(2a\) along the rod from \(A\). Both contacts are at limiting equilibrium, with \(A\) about to move away from the wall and \(B\) about to move down. The ground coefficient of friction is \(1/4\).

(a) [6]

Find both normal reactions and both frictional forces.

(b) [3]

Find the coefficient of friction at the wall.

(c) [3]

Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant contact force at \(B\).
original.hint_html: Both friction forces oppose the specified impending movements. Include the wall friction when taking moments.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(N_A=6W/5,\ R_B=3W/10,\ F_A=3W/10\) towards the wall, \(F_B=3W/10\) upwards.

(b)

\(\mu_B=1\).

(c)

\(3\sqrt2W/10\), at \(45^\circ\) above the horizontal away from the wall.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Friction at \(A\) acts towards the wall and friction at \(B\) acts upwards. Let \(N_A\) be the upward ground normal and \(R_B\) the horizontal wall normal. Then \[F_A=\frac14N_A,\qquad R_B=F_A,\qquad N_A+F_B=\frac32W.\] The rod centre and particle have horizontal distances \(3a/2\) and \(6a/5\) from \(A\). Taking moments about \(A\), \[4aR_B+3aF_B=\frac32aW+\frac12W\frac{6a}{5}=\frac{21}{10}aW.\] Substitute \(R_B=N_A/4\), \(F_B=3W/2-N_A\): \[N_A+\frac92W-3N_A=\frac{21}{10}W,\] so \(N_A=6W/5\), and the other three forces each have magnitude \(3W/10\). All assumed directions are confirmed.

Part (b)

Because the wall contact is also limiting, \[\mu_B=\frac{F_B}{R_B}=\frac{3W/10}{3W/10}=1.\] The ground normal must not be used in this ratio: each friction force has its own contact normal.

Part (c)

The wall force has equal horizontal and upward components, each \(3W/10\). Its magnitude is \[\sqrt{R_B^2+F_B^2}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{10}W.\] It is directed away from the wall and upwards, at \(45^\circ\) to the horizontal.

The horizontal separation \(AD\) is \(5a\cos\theta\). Project \(AD\) onto the rod: \(AC=AD\cos\theta=5a\cos^2\theta\). Since \(\tan\theta=2\), \(\cos^2\theta=1/5\), so \(AC=a\).

(b) [3]

Part (a)

Use \(\rho\pi a^2h\) as a mass unit. The full cylinder has mass \(1\), centre \(h/2\) below the top. The removed cylinder has mass \(k/4\), centre \(kh/2\) below the top. Hence \[d=\frac{h/2-(k/4)(kh/2)}{1-k/4}=\frac{h(4-k^2)}{2(4-k)}.\] By axial symmetry there is no horizontal offset from the cylinder axis.

Part (b)

From the suspension point to the centre there is an axial separation \(d\) and a radial separation \(a\). Since \(AB\) lies in the top face, \(\tan\theta=d/a\). (b) [4]

original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The hemisphere and cylinder volumes are \(18\pi a^3\) and \(\pi a^2d\). Their centres are \((3a,-9a/8)\) and \((a,d/2)\). Cancelling the common density and \(\pi a^2\), \[\bar x=\frac{18a(3a)+d(a)}{18a+d}=\frac{a(54a+d)}{18a+d},\] \[\bar y=\frac{18a(-9a/8)+d(d/2)}{18a+d}=\frac{2d^2-81a^2}{4(18a+d)}.\]

Part (b)

With only weight and the contact force acting, their lines of action must coincide. The contact point lies vertically below \(G\). For a plane rising leftwards, the contact point is \(3a\sin\theta\) to the left of \(C\). Its horizontal coordinate is therefore \(3a-3a/5=12a/5\).

Set \(\bar x=12a/5\): \[\frac{54a+d}{18a+d}=\frac{12}{5}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad270a+5d=216a+12d.\] Thus \(d=54a/7\). This is positive. The contact resultant must be vertical, so preventing slip requires at least \(\mu\ge\tan\theta=1/(2\sqrt6)\); sufficient friction was assumed. A uniform solid cylinder of radius \(4r\) and height \(3r\), made of the same material, is attached to the cone's base with coincident axes. You may use that the centre of a uniform solid cone is three quarters of its height from its vertex. The assembly is placed with one complete straight generator of the cone in contact with a horizontal plane.

(a) [4]

Find the distance of the centre of mass from the free circular end of the cylinder.

(b) [3]

Show that equilibrium is possible in this position by locating the vertical projection of the centre of mass on the contacting generator.
original.hint_html: The relevant base is the contacting generator, not the cone’s circular face.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(33r/16\).

(b)

The projection is \(189r/80\) from the vertex, strictly between \(0\) and \(5r\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Measure along the axis from the cone vertex \(V\). The cone and cylinder volumes are \(16\pi r^3\) and \(48\pi r^3\), and their centres are \(9r/4\) and \(9r/2\) from \(V\). Hence \[VG=\frac{16(9r/4)+48(9r/2)}{64}=\frac{63r}{16}.\] The free cylinder end is \(6r\) from \(V\), so the required distance is \(6r-63r/16=33r/16\).

Part (b)

The generator has length \(\sqrt{(3r)^2+(4r)^2}=5r\). If its angle with the axis is \(\beta\), then \(\cos\beta=3/5\). Since the generator is horizontal, the vertical projection of \(G\) lies at distance \[VG\cos\beta=\frac{63r}{16}\frac35=\frac{189r}{80}\] from the vertex along that generator. This is strictly between its endpoints \(0\) and \(5r\). An upward support resultant through this point balances the weight with zero net moment. No friction is required on a horizontal plane. This establishes possible equilibrium, not a statement about stability against every perturbation.

original.stem_html: A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(5a\) and weight \(W\), is hinged to a vertical wall at \(A=(0,0)\). It is held with \(B=(4a,3a)\). A particle of weight \(W/2\) is fixed at \(B\). A light elastic string joins \(C\), the point on the rod with \(AC=3a\), to \(D=(0,5a)\) on the wall.
original.question_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(5a\) and weight \(W\), is hinged to a vertical wall at \(A=(0,0)\). It is held with \(B=(4a,3a)\). A particle of weight \(W/2\) is fixed at \(B\). A light elastic string joins \(C\), the point on the rod with \(AC=3a\), to \(D=(0,5a)\) on the wall.

(a) [3]

Show that the string is perpendicular to the rod and find its tension.

(b) [4]

Find the magnitude and direction of the hinge reaction.

(c) [4]

The natural length of the string is \(3a\). Find its modulus of elasticity.
original.hint_html: Take moments about the hinge, then resolve forces; use extension rather than actual length in Hooke’s law.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(CD=4a,\quad T=4W/3\).

(b)

\(R=\sqrt{745}W/30\), at \(\tan^{-1}(13/24)\) above the horizontal away from the wall.

(c)

\(\lambda=4W\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Since the rod has direction ratios \(4:3\), \(C=(12a/5,9a/5)\). From \(C\) to \(D\), the horizontal and vertical displacements are \(-12a/5\) and \(16a/5\), so \(CD=4a\). The string has direction ratios \(-3:4\), perpendicular to \(4:3\).

Its moment about \(A\) is therefore \(3aT\). The downward loads have moment \(W(2a)+(W/2)(4a)=4Wa\). Hence \(3aT=4Wa\), giving \(T=4W/3\).

Part (b)

The cable components are \(-3T/5\) and \(4T/5\). Thus the hinge components are \[H=\frac35T=\frac45W,\qquad V=\frac32W-\frac45T=\frac{13}{30}W.\] Both are positive in the rightward and upward directions. Consequently \[R=W\sqrt{\left(\frac45\right)^2+\left(\frac{13}{30}\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{745}}{30}W,\qquad\tan\phi=\frac{V}{H}=\frac{13}{24}.\]

Part (c)

The actual length is \(4a\), so the extension is \(a\), not \(4a\). Hooke's law gives \[T=\frac{\lambda e}{l}=\frac{\lambda a}{3a}=\frac{\lambda}{3}.\] Using \(T=4W/3\) gives \(\lambda=4W\). The extension and tension are positive, so the string is taut as assumed.

original.question_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(5a\) and weight \(W\), is hinged at \(A=(0,0)\) and held with \(B=(3a,-4a)\). A light elastic string joins \(B\) to \(O=(9a,4a)\). Its natural length is \(8a\). The rod and string lie in one vertical plane.

(a) [3]

Find the string tension.

(b) [3]

Find the modulus of elasticity.

(c) [4]

Find the angle and direction of the hinge force relative to the horizontal.
original.hint_html: Because B is below A, both components of the cable tension have moments in the same sense.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(T=5W/16\).

(b)

\(\lambda=5W/4\).

(c)

\(\tan^{-1}4\) above the horizontal towards the left.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The string has displacement \((6a,8a)\) from \(B\), so its length is \(10a\), and its force components are \(3T/5\) rightwards and \(4T/5\) upwards. Their total anticlockwise moment about \(A\) is \[(3a)\frac{4T}{5}+(4a)\frac{3T}{5}=\frac{24aT}{5}.\] The rod weight acts at horizontal distance \(3a/2\). Equating moments gives \(24aT/5=3aW/2\), hence \(T=5W/16\).

Part (b)

The extension is \(10a-8a=2a\). Thus \(T=\lambda(2a)/(8a)=\lambda/4\). With \(T=5W/16\), the modulus is \(\lambda=5W/4\).

Part (c)

The hinge must oppose the rightward cable component, so \(H=-3T/5=-3W/16\). Its vertical component is \(V=W-4T/5=3W/4\). Thus the force points upwards and leftwards. Relative to the leftward horizontal, \[\tan\phi=\frac{3W/4}{3W/16}=4,\] so \(\phi=\tan^{-1}4\). Stating only an unsigned tangent would not identify the correct direction.

A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(5a\) and weight \(2W\), is hinged to a wall at \(A=(0,0)\) and held with \(B=(4a,3a)\). A ring of weight \(W\) is at \(P=(a,7a)\) on a rough horizontal wire through \(Q=(0,7a)\). A light elastic string joins \(B\) to \(P\), and has natural length \(4a\). The ring is in limiting equilibrium. All forces and lengths are in the same vertical plane.

(a) [3]

Find the string tension.

(b) [2]

Find the coefficient of friction between ring and wire.

(c) [3]

Find the magnitude of the hinge reaction on the rod.

(d) [2]

Find the modulus of elasticity of the string.
original.hint_html: Draw separate force diagrams for the rod and the ring; the string forces have opposite directions.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The string displacement from \(B\) is \((-3a,4a)\), so its length is \(5a\). It is perpendicular to the rod direction \((4,3)\). Moments about the hinge give \(5aT=2W(2a)\), hence \(T=4W/5\).

Part (b)

On the ring, tension acts towards \(B\), with components \(3T/5\) rightwards and \(4T/5\) downwards. Therefore friction is \(12W/25\) leftwards and the wire normal is \(W+16W/25=41W/25\) upwards. Thus \(\mu=(12/25)/(41/25)=12/41\).

Part (c)

On the rod, the string pulls leftwards and upwards. The hinge components are therefore \[H=\frac35T=\frac{12}{25}W,\qquad V=2W-\frac45T=\frac{34}{25}W.\] Consequently \(R=W\sqrt{12^2+34^2}/25=2\sqrt{13}W/5\).

Part (d)

The string's extension is \(5a-4a=a\). Hooke's law gives \(T=\lambda/4\), so \(\lambda=4T=16W/5\). The string is stretched, as required.

A uniform square lamina has side \(4a\) and weight \(W\). Its vertex \(B\) rests on rough horizontal ground. The side \(BA\) runs upwards to the left and makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal, with \(\tan\theta=1/2\). The square lies to the upper-right of this side. A smooth peg touches \(BA\) at \(E\), where \(BE=3a\), and pushes perpendicular to \(BA\), upwards and to the right. The lamina is in a vertical plane.

(a) [5]

Find the normal reaction \(R\) at the peg, the normal reaction \(N\) at the ground, and the friction at \(B\).

(b) [3]

Find the coefficient of friction if the lamina is just about to slip.
original.hint_html: The square’s centre is displaced both along and perpendicular to the supported side.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write \(s=\sin\theta=1/\sqrt5\), \(c=\cos\theta=2/\sqrt5\). Relative to \(B\), the centre of mass has horizontal coordinate \(2a(s-c)\). The peg reaction has components \((Rs,Rc)\). Its clockwise moment about \(B\) is \(3aR\), while the weight gives anticlockwise moment \(2aW(c-s)\). Thus \[3aR=2aW(c-s),\qquad R=\frac{2W}{3\sqrt5}.\] Vertical balance gives \(N=W-Rc=11W/15\). Horizontal balance requires friction \(Rs=2W/15\) to the left. All normal reactions are positive.

Part (b)

At limiting equilibrium \(F=\mu N\). Therefore \[\mu=\frac{2W/15}{11W/15}=\frac2{11}.\] The peg is smooth, so no tangential force is included there. The single friction force is at \(B\).

A smooth peg touches the rod at \(C\), where \(AC=x\), and pushes perpendicular to the rod, upwards and to the left. The coefficient of friction at \(A\) is \(\mu\gt0\). The rod is in limiting equilibrium, with \(0\lt x\le8a\).

(a) [4]

Express \(x\) in terms of \(a\) and \(\mu\).

(b) [3]

Deduce a lower bound for \(\mu\).

(c) [4]

If \(x=4a\), find \(\mu\) and the magnitude of the resultant contact force at \(A\).
original.hint_html: The peg position is restricted by the length of the rod, and the ground normal must stay non-negative.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the peg reaction be \(R\). Moment balance about \(A\) gives \(Rx=4aW\cos\theta\). Thus \(R=16aW/(5x)\). The ground forces are \[F=R\sin\theta=\frac{48aW}{25x},\qquad N=W-R\cos\theta=W\left(1-\frac{64a}{25x}\right).\] At limiting equilibrium \(F=\mu N\), so \(48a=\mu(25x-64a)\). Hence \(x=a(64+48/\mu)/25\).

Part (b)

The peg must lie on the rod, so \(x\le8a\). Substitute the result from part (a): \(64+48/\mu\le200\). Since \(\mu\gt0\), this gives \(\mu\ge48/136=6/17\). The formula also gives \(x\gt64a/25\), so the ground normal reaction is positive.

Part (c)

At \(x=4a\), the peg reaction is \(4W/5\). Therefore \(F=12W/25\) and \(N=9W/25\). Thus \[\mu=\frac{12}{9}=\frac43,\qquad R_A=\sqrt{F^2+N^2}=\frac{15W}{25}=\frac35W.\] The ground resultant acts upwards and to the right.

Part (a)

Write \(s=\sin\alpha\), \(c=\cos\alpha\). Relative to \(K\), the centre is at horizontal coordinate \(-as\), and \(P\) is at height \(a(c+s)\). Two identical uniform rods \(AB\) and \(BC\), each of length \(2a\) and weight \(W\), are rigidly joined at right angles at \(B\). They rest against a fixed rough cylinder of radius \(a\), with the midpoint \(D\) of \(AB\) and midpoint \(E\) of \(BC\) as the contact points. The bracket lies in a vertical plane perpendicular to the cylinder axis. The rod direction from \(A\) to \(B\) is \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), with \(0\lt\theta\lt\pi/4\). Relative to the cylinder centre, \(D=(-a\sin\theta,a\cos\theta)\) and \(E=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta)\). Both contacts have coefficient of friction \(\mu\), with \(0\lt\mu\lt1\), and the bracket is about to slip clockwise. Normal reactions at \(D\) and \(E\) are \(R\) and \(N\).

(a) [4]

Show that \(R:N=(1+\mu):(1-\mu)\).

(b) [5]

Given \(\mu=1/4\), find \(\tan\theta\), and check that the normal reactions are positive.
original.hint_html: Use the whole rigid bracket. Friction at the two contacts has different directions but the same rotational sense about the cylinder centre.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(s=\sin\theta\), \(c=\cos\theta\). The outward normals at \(D\) and \(E\) have directions \((-s,c)\) and \((c,s)\). To oppose clockwise slipping, friction at \(D\) acts along \((-c,-s)\), and at \(E\) along \((-s,c)\). Resolving parallel to the two rods gives \[N-\mu R=2Ws,\qquad R+\mu N=2Wc.\] Taking moments about the cylinder centre, both friction moments are anticlockwise, while the combined weight moment is \(Wa(s-c)\). Hence \[\mu(R+N)=W(c-s).\] From the two force equations, \(2W(c-s)=(1+\mu)R-(1-\mu)N\). Substitute this into the moment equation and rearrange: \[(1-\mu)R=(1+\mu)N.\] This gives the required ratio.

Part (b)

The ratio becomes \(R/N=5/3\); write \(R=5q\), \(N=3q\). The force equations give \[2Ws=3q-\frac54q=\frac74q,\qquad2Wc=5q+\frac34q=\frac{23}{4}q.\] Divide to obtain \(\tan\theta=7/23\), which is in \((0,1)\). Also \(c\gt0\) gives \(q=8Wc/23\gt0\), so \(R,N\gt0\). Both specified contacts are physically admissible.

Find the cylinder reaction \(R\) in terms of \(k\) and \(W\).

(b) [4]

original.hint_html: Only the component of the cylinder reaction normal to the floor contributes to the ground normal balance.

The reaction is perpendicular to the rod, so its moment arm about \(A\) is \(4a\). The rod weight acts \(3a\) along the rod and the particle at \(6a\). Therefore \[4aR=W(3a)\frac45+kW(6a)\frac45,\] which gives \(R=3(1+2k)W/5\).

Hence \(k=4/17\). Substitution gives \(N=F=9W/17\gt0\), and \(R=15W/17\gt0\), so no contact is lost.
